title: Rachel wanted to be chosen.
paragraphs:
Rachel wanted to be chosen.
Leah wanted to be seen.
And between them stood one man who could not heal what only God could touch.
Genesis 29 is not just a story about sisters. It is a mirror. A house full of longing. A marriage built through deception. A rivalry fed by pain. A love story already bleeding before it begins.
Jacob loved Rachel. Scripture does not soften it. “Jacob loved Rachel,” and later, “he loved Rachel more than Leah” (Genesis 29:18, 30). Read that again.
That one line explains so much of the sorrow that followed.

Leah entered the marriage unwanted. Rachel entered it adored. But here’s what most people don’t realize: being unloved did not save Leah, and being loved did not save Rachel. One was crushed by rejection. The other was consumed by comparison. Both were wounded. Both were striving. Both were looking for something in human love that only God can provide.
And that is where the whole scene turns.

Scripture says, “When the Lord saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb, but Rachel was barren” (Genesis 29:31). God saw the woman no one really saw. The overlooked one. The unwanted one. The one living in the shadow of her sister and the preference of her husband.

Leah kept bearing sons, and with each child you can hear the ache in her words. “Because the Lord has looked upon my affliction… now my husband will love me” (Genesis 29:32). Then again, “Because the Lord has heard that I am hated” (Genesis 29:33). Then again, “Now this time my husband will be attached to me” (Genesis 29:34).
Do you hear it?

She was naming children from a place of pain. Hoping each blessing would finally earn the love she had never received. Hoping the next thing would fix the old wound. Hoping attachment could heal rejection.
That is not just Leah’s story. That is ours.

We chase approval. We compete for affection. We measure our worth by who notices us, chooses us, praises us, desires us. Sin does this. It bends the heart inward. It teaches us to worship acceptance. It trains us to believe that if we are loved enough by people, we will finally be whole.

But Scripture says otherwise: “All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). The deepest crisis in Rachel and Leah’s story is not just family dysfunction. It is the human condition. A broken heart in a fallen world. Desire disordered by sin. Identity attached to idols. Love turned into a throne.
And idols always wound the people who bow to them.

Originally written by Gospel Warrior, this is where the story stops being ancient and starts becoming personal. Because some of you are Leah—trying to earn love that should have been freely given. Some of you are Rachel—afraid that even being desired will not be enough. Some of you are Jacob—blind to the damage caused by favoritism, manipulation, and flesh-driven love.
Then something astonishing happens in Leah’s grief. With her fourth son, the language changes. She says, “This time I will praise the Lord” (Genesis 29:35).
This time.

Not, “Now my husband will love me.”
Not, “Now I will be enough.”
Not, “Now I will win.”
“This time I will praise the Lord.”
That is the turning point. The wound is still there. The marriage is still broken. The rivalry is not over. But Leah’s eyes begin to lift above human approval and toward God Himself.
But even that is not the final answer.
Because Genesis 29 exposes the wound, but only Jesus heals it.

Leah could not save herself by bearing sons. Rachel could not save herself by being beautiful. Jacob could not save himself by passion. You cannot save yourself by being chosen, admired, productive, attractive, spiritual, or strong. “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick” (Jeremiah 17:9). That sickness runs deeper than romance. Deeper than family pain. Deeper than rejection.
So God sent Christ.

“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).
“In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses” (Ephesians 1:7).
“For by grace you have been saved through faith… not a result of works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9).

This is the Gospel: you do not need to compete for the love of God. In Christ, repentant sinners are received by grace. Jesus lived the life you could not live, died the death your sin deserved, and rose again so that the rejected, the bitter, the jealous, the proud, the broken, and the ashamed could be made new.
And here is the mercy hidden inside Leah’s tears: from her line would come Judah, and through Judah would come the Messiah. The unloved woman was placed in the lineage of Christ. Read that again.
The world may rank people by beauty, preference, status, and attention. But God writes redemption through the dismissed.
That is why this story matters.

Not because sister rivalry is dramatic.
Not because broken love is relatable.
But because God meets sinners in the wreckage and points to Jesus.

So repent. Stop asking human love to do what only Christ can do. Stop making an idol of being chosen. Stop drinking from cracked wells. Come to the Savior who does not love selectively, temporarily, or selfishly. Come to the One who says, “Whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).
This post is only the surface. Go deeper here:

So here’s the question:
Are you still competing for a love that can never save you, or are you ready to rest in the love of Christ?
